hints: Look at the central carbon in the diagram and remember R can be small and simple or a bit larger, but for the 20 amino acids used to make proteins it is never huge.
Compare each option to amino acids you know, like alanine with $CH_3$, and ask yourself which one looks like a 3-carbon sugar with three -OH groups instead of a normal R group.
walkthrough:
**Recall what R means**

Think of the diagram as the common backbone shared by all amino acids. The $NH_2$, central $C$ with $H$, and $COOH$ are always the same.

Only R changes, and there are just 20 different R groups used to make proteins.

**Spot the familiar R groups**

$CH_3$ is the tiny methyl group of alanine. $CH_2CH_2SCH_3$ is the sulfur-containing R of methionine. $CH_2CONH_2$ is the amide-containing R of asparagine.

All three are small, real side chains you meet in 9700.

**Spot the odd one out**

$HOCH_2CH(OH)CH_2OH$ has three carbons and three hydroxyl (-OH) groups. That is far too large and too full of -OH groups for any of the 20 standard amino acids.

It looks more like part of a carbohydrate like glycerol, not an amino acid R group, so it is not possible.

options.A: This is possible. $CH_3$ is the R group of alanine, one of the simplest amino acids.
options.B: This is possible. $CH_2CH_2SCH_3$ is the sulfur-containing R group of methionine.
options.C: This is possible. $CH_2CONH_2$ is the amide R group of asparagine.
options.D: This is not possible. No standard amino acid has this large 3-carbon, 3-hydroxyl side chain.
